lead: Levelling finds how much higher or lower one point is than another. A level cannot measure a height above the sea directly: it gives a horizontal line of sight, and two staff readings taken from one set-up give the height difference between the two staff points. Heights become useful only when every difference is tied to one agreed zero surface, the datum, through a point whose height is already known, the benchmark. The height of any point above the datum is its reduced level. Road gradients, drain slopes, canal beds, plinth levels and contour maps are all built from these three ideas.

blocks.text: A level surface is everywhere at right angles to gravity, like the surface of still water; because the earth is round, it is curved. A level line is a line on a level surface, so it is curved too.

A horizontal plane at a point is the flat plane that touches the level surface at that point. A horizontal line is a straight line in that plane, and a vertical line is the direction of a plumb bob, at right angles to the level surface. With the bubble centred, a level's line of collimation (through the cross-hairs and the objective's centre) is horizontal. Over sights of about 100 m the horizontal and level lines differ by under a millimetre; longer sights need the curvature and refraction correction.

The datum is the level surface from which heights are measured. National maps use mean sea level (MSL), the average sea level over a long period of tide readings; the Survey of India publishes benchmark heights above it. A small site may use an arbitrary datum (say, a gate pillar called 100.000 m); such heights compare with each other but not with a map until the datums are connected.

The reduced level (RL) of a point is its height above the datum, in metres, usually written to three decimals (millimetres). Some syllabi call it the elevation of the point. A point below the datum has a negative RL; for example the floor of a deep sump on an arbitrary datum of 0.000 m at the road can have RL −2.350 m. Always write the datum beside a height, because a height without its datum is not an RL.
A benchmark (BM) is a fixed, well-marked point whose RL is known. Four kinds are named in the syllabi:

items: GTS benchmark: a mark of the Great Trigonometrical Survey across the country, with its RL above MSL published by the Survey of India; the most reliable starting height.
Permanent benchmark: a mark fixed by a department such as PWD or the railways on a culvert, pier or milestone, its RL found from a GTS benchmark.
Arbitrary benchmark: a point given an assumed RL (for example 100.000 m) on a small job where no permanent benchmark is near; all heights are then relative.
Temporary benchmark (TBM): a point fixed for one job, such as a peg in concrete or a mark on a kerb, used to close the day's work and to restart from the next day.

blocks.text: A station is the point where the staff is held and a reading is taken. The levelling staff is a graduated rod held vertically on the station; the reading where the horizontal cross-hair cuts it is the height of the line of collimation above the foot of the staff.

sections.h3: The readings and the height chain

blocks.text: Each set-up of the level has one backsight (BS): the first reading, taken on a point of known RL. It may have several intermediate sights (IS): readings on points whose RL is wanted. It ends with one foresight (FS): the last reading before the instrument is moved. A change point (CP), also called a turning point, is a firm station that takes a foresight from one set-up and then a backsight from the next, so the height chain carries across the move.
The height of instrument (HI), also called the height of collimation, is the RL of the line of collimation for one set-up. It is a reduced level, not the height of the tripod above the ground.
HI = RL of the backsight station + BS;   RL of any station = HI − its staff reading
blocks.where: All values are in metres. The BS and the reading on the new station must come from the same set-up, because each set-up has its own HI.

blocks.text: Combining the two gives RL(new) = RL(known) + BS − FS. A positive BS − FS means the new point is higher than the known point. A large reading means low ground, because more of the staff stands below the line of sight.

examples.question: A level is set up near a road culvert. The permanent benchmark on the culvert has RL 120.450 m above MSL. The staff readings are: 1.865 m on the BM, 0.635 m on the plinth of a building, 2.410 m on the road edge, and 1.250 m on a peg to be used as a TBM (the last reading before the level is moved). (a) Name each reading. (b) Find the HI and the RL of the plinth, the road edge and the TBM. (c) The site drawings had used an arbitrary datum, calling the plinth 100.000 m. Convert the arbitrary RLs 101.385 m and 98.640 m to MSL.
steps: (a) 1.865 m on the BM is the backsight (first reading, on a known RL). 0.635 m and 2.410 m are intermediate sights. 1.250 m on the peg is the foresight, because it is the last reading before the level moves.
RL of road edge = 122.315 − 2.410 = 119.905 m. The large reading tells us the road is the lowest point seen.
Check: RL(TBM) − RL(BM) should equal BS − FS. 121.065 − 120.450 = 0.615 m and 1.865 − 1.250 = 0.615 m. They agree.
(c) The plinth is 100.000 m on the arbitrary datum and 121.680 m on MSL, so the MSL value = arbitrary value + 21.680 m.
examples.answer: HI = 122.315 m; RL of plinth 121.680 m, road edge 119.905 m, TBM 121.065 m (all above MSL). The arbitrary heights 101.385 m and 98.640 m are 123.065 m and 120.320 m above MSL.

traps: Calling the HI the height of the tripod. HI is the RL of the line of sight: 122.315 m in the example, not about 1.5 m.
Mixing readings of two set-ups in RL = RL(known) + BS − FS. The BS and the FS must be read with the instrument in the same place.
Thinking a larger reading means a higher point. It is the opposite: a larger staff reading means lower ground.
Leaving out the datum. Write “RL 121.680 m above MSL” or “on an arbitrary datum”; two heights on different datums cannot be subtracted.

quiz.q: Define datum, benchmark and reduced level.
quiz.a: Datum: the level surface from which heights are measured (usually MSL). Benchmark: a fixed point of known RL. Reduced level: the height of a point above the datum.

quiz.q: Distinguish a level line from a horizontal line.
quiz.a: A level line lies on a level surface and curves with the earth. A horizontal line is straight and touches the level line at one point; the line of sight of a levelled instrument is a horizontal line.

quiz.q: What is a change point, and why must it be on firm ground?
quiz.a: A station read as a foresight from one set-up and as a backsight from the next. It carries the RL across the move, so if the staff sinks or shifts between the two readings every later RL is wrong.

quiz.q: The BS on a BM of RL 245.300 m is 0.875 m and the FS on a point P is 2.940 m (same set-up). Find the HI and the RL of P.
A sump floor reads 3.620 m from a set-up whose HI is 101.270 m on an arbitrary datum of 100.000 m at the road. Find its RL and say what the sign means.
quiz.a: RL = 101.270 − 3.620 = 97.650 m. It is positive on this datum; on a datum taken as 0.000 m at the road it would be −2.350 m, that is 2.350 m below the road.

quiz.q: A student books the FS on the TBM as 1.520 m instead of 1.250 m in the worked example. What happens to the TBM RL and to the next day's work?
quiz.a: RL(TBM) becomes 122.315 − 1.520 = 120.795 m, 0.270 m too low. Every RL carried forward from that TBM next day is also 0.270 m too low, and only a closing check on a second benchmark will show it.

beyond: Not for the exam. A GNSS receiver gives heights above a mathematical ellipsoid (WGS 84), not above mean sea level; a geoid model converts one to the other, and the difference across India runs to tens of metres. National agencies are moving from benchmark networks on the ground to geoid-based height systems that GNSS can use directly. Digital levels read a bar-coded staff and store the RLs, but the datum and benchmark logic is unchanged. Search for orthometric height, geoid undulation and vertical datum.

figure.caption: The worked example in section. The backsight on the benchmark lifts the height to the line of collimation (HI 122.315 m); each staff reading is then subtracted from the HI. The RLs are heights above mean sea level, which is drawn with a break because it is far below.
